title: Mono: .NET without Microsoft
sub: How C# reached Linux long before .NET Core
cards/0/title: An open standard invites new implementations
cards/0/body:
Microsoft submitted the C# and CLI specs to ECMA as a standard. That meant anyone could write their own runtime from the spec.

Miguel de Icaza and his company Ximian did exactly that: in 2004 they released Mono 1.0, .NET for Linux.
cards/1/task: Find the year Mono 1.0 came out and see where you could now run C#.
cards/2/q: How could Mono be built without Microsoft's source code?
cards/2/options/0: C# and the CLI are described in an open ECMA standard
cards/2/options/2: Mono is just a renamed Framework
cards/2/explain: It is an independent implementation of an open spec.
cards/3/body:
Novell bought Ximian (2003). In 2011 Novell laid off the team, and they founded Xamarin: C# for iOS and Android, built on Mono. In 2016 Microsoft bought Xamarin.

In 2024 Microsoft handed the Mono project over to the WineHQ community. The Mono runtime also lives on inside modern .NET, for mobile platforms and WebAssembly.
cards/4/explain: Mono started in 2001, Novell bought Ximian in 2003, Xamarin was founded in 2011, Microsoft bought it in 2016, and WineHQ took over in 2024.
cards/5/q: Where did Mono run? Select all that apply.
cards/5/explain: Linux and macOS were the whole point. Unity also embedded it in its engine.
cards/6/q: Match each name to what it is
cards/7/q: What does the Mono runtime do inside modern .NET today?
cards/7/options/0: Runs .NET on mobile platforms and in WebAssembly
cards/7/explain: It is small, so it fits well where CoreCLR is too heavy.
